Parhon” National Institute of Endocrinology, 2”Carol Davila” University of Medicine - Endocrinology, 3Central Military University Emergency Hospital - Department of Endocrinology, 4”Fundeni” Hospital - Department of Hematology, 5”Carol Davila” University of Medicine, Faculty of Medicine - Division of Hematology, Bucharest, Romania, 6Mayo Clinic - Endocrinology, Rochester, Minnesota, United States of America Abstract Primary bilateral adrenal lymphoma is a very rare cause of adrenal insufficiency.   We report the case of a 63year-old woman who presented with signs and symptoms of impending adrenal crisis when referred for evaluation of large bilateral adrenal masses diagnosed on a computed tomography scan two weeks prior.   Based on a high clinical suspicion of adrenal insufficiency, patient was initiated on glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid therapy prior to laboratory confirmation of adrenal insufficiency.

After stabilizing the patient and excluding pheochromocytoma, we proceeded with adrenal biopsy that revealed a nongerminal centertype diffuse large Bcell lymphoma.   Our patient was treated with RCHOP chemotherapy, with good response after 3 cycles but eventually died after the fifth cycle from neurologic complications. This case highlights the notion that primary adrenal insufficiency should be considered in patients presenting with bilateral adrenal masses.

Although primary adrenal lymphoma is a very rare adrenal malignancy it should be considered in patients presenting with bilateral rapidly growing adrenal tumors and primary adrenal insufficiency. Keywords: adrenal lymphoma, adrenal crisis, adrenal biopsy. INTRODUCTION Primary adrenal lymphoma (PAL) is a very rare adrenal malignancy with a prevalence of 0.2% of all adrenal masses (1) and 25% of all adrenal malignancies (2, 3).

Bilateral involvement of adrenal glands in patients with primary adrenal lymphoma was reported in up to 30% of cases (2) and may be associated with adrenal insufficiency (4).   Once established, primary adrenal insufficiency is usually permanent (5, 6).   The most common subtype of PAL is diffuse large B cell lymphoma, with a generally poor prognosis.

We report a case of PAL presenting as impending adrenal crisis. CASE PRESENTATION A 63year-old woman was referred to our Endocrinology Department for the evaluation of bilateral large adrenal masses detected on a computed tomography (CT) scan performed two weeks prior to presentation for evaluation of unexplained weight loss and general sense of malaise. She reported symptoms of fatigue, anorexia, nausea, weight loss, and muscle weakness for two months prior to presentation.

She noticed improvement in her blood pressure and glucose control without any changes in diet or pharmacotherapy.   Her past medical history included hypertension, chronic heart failure, type 2 diabetes mellitus, recurrent atrial fibrillation on chronic anticoagulation (acenocoumarol), and history of total hysterectomy performed for an endometrioma two years prior.   On examination, her blood pressure was 100/65 mmHg while she was seated but dropped to 80/60 mmHg after she stood up.

Her heart rate was regular at 90 beats per minute, her body mass index was 36.7 kg/m2, and temperature was 37¯C. She appeared to be in distress, was unable to stand without help, and had mild skin hyperpigmentation and moderate peripheral edema. Bilateral flank masses were palpated.

Concomitant mineralocorticoid deficiency was diagnosed based on low levels of aldosterone, high renin, and hyponatremia (Table 1). CT of the abdomen revealed large bilateral adrenal masses measuring 98 ×126 mm on the left and 86 × 118 mm on the right (Fig.

1 A, B) without lymphadenopathy. Both adrenal lesions were solid and heterogeneous, suggestive of hemorrhagic necrosis and demonstrated a moderate postcontrast enhancement.   Both kidneys were displaced downwards and could not be easily separated from adjacent structures: the diaphragmatic crus, tail of the pancreas, some segments of the liver; both adrenal masses appeared to encase homolateral renal hilum.

The renal vasculature and inferior vena cava were displaced but with normal flux.   Percutaneous ultrasoundguided core biopsy of the right adrenal mass was performed using a semiautomatic 18gauge needle.
